Noticing his unmarried son, they offered the swine-herd’s daughter to him in marriage. In due course, their cleverly planned foolishness became habitual, and habit became second nature to them: “Consuetudo est altera natura.” In the end, they found that they could not be other than the fools they had become. Fear of a cat (a “mousedog”) led them finally to burn down their whole town and to scatter to the four corners of the world, spreading their folly to every tribe of the race of man: “And so the name and tribe of Lalen from Laleburg disappeared and was extinguished. And yet their nonsense and folly, which was their best part, survived. Perhaps you and I have even inherited a good portion of it. Who knows if it’s not true?” $ ^{1} $

matched_examples.note_excerpt: Folk-book can be a dangerous term if it is taken to mean a book with no author, a book that therefore springs directly from the timeless soul of the people. Hans Joachim Kreutzer has provided a trenchant warning against such romanticizing tendencies in Der Mythos vom Volksbuch (Stuttgart, 1977). In recent years, the authorship and even the priority of the Lalebuch (the assumption that it came before the Schildbiirgerbuch) have been questioned, in a dispute that need not detain us. Rupert Kalkofen provides a useful analysis in “Lalebuch oder Schiltbiirger, Anonymus oder Fischart? Die buchgeschichtlichen Untersuchungen von Peter Honegger und Stefan Ertz im Vergleich,” Wirkendes Wort: Deutsche Sprache und Literatur in Forschung und Lehre 41 (1991): 363-77. The best general discussion of the wide range of research concerning this stream of German literature is Werner Wunderlich, “ “Schildbiirgerstreiche’: Bericht zur Lalebuch- und Schildbiirgerforschung,” Deutsche Vierteljahrsschrift fiir Literaturwissenschaft und Geistesgeschichte 56 (1982): 641-85.
matched_examples.anchor_excerpt: one of the best-selling “folk-books” of early modern Germany. $ ^{2} $ For some readers, the fun lay in thinking of a place of such resounding stupidity: many cultures tell such stories, after all. $ ^{3} $ For others, the dystopia of the Lalen and Schildbürger allows us to feel the frustration of humanistically educated burghers increasingly exploited by the selfish demands of expanding princely courts. $ ^{4} $ But it is just as true that the Lalebuch can be seen as a rewriting of the fall of man, a fall not into sin and perversion but into folly. And in this sense, the fools of Laleburg can stand as emblems of a century that had revealed in folly as the lively image of all that was wrong in life, and sometimes of all that was right.
